Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 25, verse 59:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days﴾.

We have already presented the verse that contains the detailed explanation of this in Surat "al-A'raf," in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾ [al-A'raf: 54].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then He istawa (rose) over the Throne, the Most Merciful. So ask about Him one who is informed﴾.

We have already presented its clarification by means of the Qur'anic verses in Surat "al-A'raf," in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then He istawa over the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], and so on.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 25, verse 60:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate yourselves to the Most Merciful," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful? Shall we prostrate to whatever you command us?" And it increases them in aversion.﴾

In this noble verse, exalted and most high is He, He mentions that when the disbelievers are told ﴿"Prostrate yourselves to the Most Merciful"⦆, that is, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims say that to them, they ignored the Most Merciful and said ﴿"And what is the Most Merciful?"﴾, and they denied prostration to Him, exalted is He, and that increased them in aversion from faith and from prostrating to the Most Merciful. What He mentions here, that they were commanded to prostrate to Him alone, exalted is He, is mentioned in other places, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate to Allah, who created them, if it is Him you worship﴾ [Fussilat: 37].

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him]﴾ [An-Najm: 62]. He also rebuked them for not complying with this in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate﴾ [Al-Inshiqaq: 21], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 48]. Their ignoring of the Most Merciful here He answered, exalted is He, with His saying: ﴿The Most Merciful. He taught the Qur'an. He created man. He taught him eloquent speech﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 1–4].

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful; whichever you call, to Him belong the most beautiful names"﴾ [Al-Isra': 110]. We have already presented a part of this in our discussion of that verse, and we have also already presented that they know that the Most Merciful is Allah, and that their ignoring of Him is the ignoring of one who knows, along with the evidences for that. As for His saying here, ﴿and it increases them in aversion﴾, its meaning has come in other places, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an that they may be reminded, but it increases them in nothing but aversion﴾ [Al-Isra': 41], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, they have persisted in arrogance and aversion﴾ [Al-Mulk: 21], among other verses.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 25, verse 61:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky great stars, and placed therein a lamp and a luminous moon.﴾

We have already presented the statements of the scholars regarding the meaning of "tabaraka" (blessed), at the beginning of this noble surah.

Al-burūj (the mansions/constellations) in the language are lofty palaces, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And even if you were in towers built up high.﴾

The scholars differed concerning what is meant by al-burūj in the verse. Some of them said: they are the great stars. Ibn Kathir said: this is the saying of Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Salih, al-Hasan, and Qatadah. Then he said: It has also been said that they are palaces in the sky for the guards. This is narrated from 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and Sulayman ibn Mihran al-A'mash, and it is also a narration from Abu Salih. The first view is more apparent, except that the great stars may be palaces for the guards, so the two views come together, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps﴾ [al-Mulk: 5]. End of the relevant point from the words of Ibn Kathir.

Al-Zamakhshari said in "al-Kashshaf": al-burūj are the stations (manāzil) of the seven wandering stars: Aries (al-Hamal), Taurus (al-Thawr), Gemini (al-Jawza'), Cancer (al-Saratan), Leo (al-Asad), Virgo (al-Sunbulah), Libra (al-Mizan), Scorpio (al-'Aqrab), Sagittarius (al-Qaws), Capricorn (al-Jady), Aquarius (al-Dalw), and Pisces (al-Hut). The burūj, which are lofty palaces, were so named because they are for these stars like dwellings for their inhabitants, and the derivation of al-burj is from al-tabarruj, meaning manifestation. End of his words.

What He, exalted and most high, mentions here, that He placed in the sky burūj and placed therein a lamp, which is the sun, and a luminous moon, He has explained in other places:

• As in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly placed in the sky burūj and adorned it for the observers﴾ [al-Hijr: 16].

• And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the sky containing burūj﴾ [al-Buruj: 1].

• And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made a blazing lamp﴾ [al-Naba': 13].

• And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not considered how Allah created seven heavens in layers? And made the moon therein a light and made the sun a lamp﴾ [Nuh: 15-16]. Most of the seven readers other than Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read this letter: ﴿and made the sun a lamp﴾ with a kasrah on the sin and a fathah on the ra' followed by an alif, in the singular. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it as surujan with a dammah on the sin and the ra', the plural of sirāj. According to the reading of the majority, with the singular sirāj, what is meant by it is the sun, as evidenced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and made the sun a lamp﴾ [Nuh: 16].

According to the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i with the plural, what is meant by the surujan is the sun and the great stars.

We have already presented in the commentary on surah al-Hijr that the apparent meaning of the Qur'an is that the moon is in the built sky, not in the sky which is simply whatever is above you, because Allah explained in surah al-Hijr that the sky in which the burūj were placed is the protected one, and the protected one is the built one, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the sky We constructed with power, and indeed, We are expanding it﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 47], and His saying: ﴿And We built above you seven strong ones﴾ [al-Naba': 12]. It is not simply whatever is above you. The explanation mentioned in surah al-Hijr in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly placed in the sky burūj and adorned it for the observers﴾ ﴿And We preserved it﴾ and so on [al-Hijr: 16-17], this verse of al-Hijr indicates that the possessor of the burūj is the built, protected one, not simply whatever is above you.

Once you know this, then know that He, exalted and most high, in this verse of al-Furqan, explained that the moon is in the sky in which He placed the burūj, because He said here: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky burūj and placed therein a lamp and a luminous moon﴾ [al-Furqan: 61]. This is evidence that it is not simply whatever is above you. This apparent meaning should not be abandoned by a Muslim except by a proof that must be returned to, from what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought.

If it is said: there occurs in the words of some of the early scholars that the moon is in a distant expanse from the sky, and that the science of astronomy (ʿilm al-hay'ah) indicates this, and that modern observations have clarified this.

We say: leaving aside consideration of the science of astronomy is acting upon the guidance of the Great Qur'an, because when the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, longed to learn the configuration of the moon from him (ﷺ) and said to him: "O Prophet of Allah, what is the matter with the crescent, that it appears thin and then continues to grow until it becomes full?" The Qur'an came down with an answer containing benefit for mankind, and left what has no benefit in it. That is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the crescents. Say: They are measurements of time for the people and for the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189]. This door, which the Great Qur'an guided us to close, when the disbelievers opened it, its result was disbelief, atheism, and denial of Allah and His Messenger, without any worldly benefit. What Allah guided us to in His Book is contemplation of the wonders of His creation and His marvels in the heavens and the earth, so that by it one may infer the perfection of His power, exalted is He, and His right to be worshipped alone. This fundamental aim was not achieved by the disbelievers who gazed at astronomy.

In any case, it is not permissible for anyone to abandon the apparent meaning of the Great Qur'an except by a convincing proof that must be returned to, as is known in its proper place.

(p-73) There is no doubt that those who attempt to ascend to the moon by their instruments, and claim that they have landed on its surface, their affair will end in the manifestation of their lowliness, weakness, incapacity, and humiliation before the power of the Creator of the heavens and the earth, exalted is He.

We have already presented in surah al-Hijr that this is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they have dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them? Then let them climb by the ropes﴾ ﴿A host of factions will be routed there﴾ [Sad: 10-11].

If it is said: the verses by which you derived that the moon is in the protected sky admit of a possibility according to a known Arabic usage, which requires that they do not indicate what you mentioned, namely the return of the pronoun to the word alone, not to the meaning.

Its clarification: it may be said that in His saying: ﴿placed in the sky burūj﴾, it is the protected sky, but the pronoun in His saying: ﴿and placed therein a lamp and a luminous moon﴾ refers to the bare word "sky," which truly applies to whatever is above you in the language. This is a known Arabic usage, expressed by the grammarians through the example: "I have a dirham and its half," meaning half of another dirham. From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And no one is granted long life or has any part of his life shortened except that it is in a Register﴾ [Fatir: 11], meaning: and no part of the life of another person is shortened.

We say: Yes, this is possible, but no proof has been established for us that obliges us to return to it, and abandoning the apparent meaning of the Great Qur'an is not permissible except by a proof that obliges return to it. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an is more deserving of following and affirmation than the sayings of the disbelievers and their imitators. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 25, verse 63:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾.

We have already presented the verses that clarify it in Surah "Bani Isra'il" (al-Isra'), in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly. Indeed, you will never tear the earth [apart], nor will you reach the mountains in height﴾ [al-Isra' 17:37].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾

We have already presented the verses that clarify it in Surah "Maryam," in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿[Abraham] said, "Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you of my Lord"﴾ and the verse [Maryam 19:47].

(p. 74) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing﴾. What He, exalted and most high, mentioned in this noble verse, that His righteous servants spend the night before their Lord prostrating and standing, worshipping Allah and praying to Him, He explained in another place:

• As in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord?﴾ [al-Zumar: 9]

• And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their sides forsake their beds, calling upon their Lord in fear and in hope﴾ [al-Sajdah: 16]

• And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed they were, before that, doers of good. They used to sleep but little of the night, and in the hours before dawn they would ask forgiveness﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 16-18]

As for His saying, exalted is He, *yabītūn* (spend the night), al-Zajjaj said: "*Bāta al-rajul yabītu*" means when the night overtakes a man, whether he sleeps or does not sleep. Zuhayr said:

"So we spent the night standing by the head of our horses, it tending to us from its own self, and we tending to it."

End of quotation via the transmission of al-Qurtubi.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 25, verse 65:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Hell; indeed, its punishment is ever adhering"﴾.

The most apparent meaning of His saying ﴿ever adhering﴾ (gharaman) is: it was constant, perpetual, never departing. From this root the creditor (al-gharim) is so named because of his persistence (mulazamah) in demanding his due. It is said: "So-and-so is mughram (ghariman) with such-and-such," meaning he is attached to it and devoted to it.

This meaning is indicated by verses from the Book of Allah, such as:

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for them is a punishment that lasts﴾ [al-Tawbah: 68]

• His saying: ﴿It will not be lightened for them, and they will be in it in despair﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 75]

• His saying: ﴿So it will be an inseparable penalty﴾ [al-Furqan: 77]

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We will not increase you except in punishment﴾ [al-Naba': 30]

• His saying: ﴿Their punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be reprieved﴾ [Al 'Imran: 88]

• His saying: ﴿Nor will its punishment be lightened for them. Thus do We recompense every ungrateful one﴾ [Fatir: 36]

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whenever it subsides, We increase them in blaze﴾ [al-Isra': 97]

• His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whenever their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment﴾ [al-Nisa': 56]

And other verses besides these.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-gharam is the most severe punishment. Ibn Zayd said: al-gharam is evil (al-sharr). Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is destruction (al-halak), as reported by al-Qurtubi. And the verse of al-A'sha:

"If He punishes, it will be gharaman, and if He gives abundantly, He does not care."

Meaning: His punishment will be perpetual and adhering. Likewise is the verse of Bishr ibn Abi Hazim:

"The Day of al-Nisar and the Day of al-Jifar, they were a punishment and they were gharaman."

And this is also the most apparent meaning in the saying of the other poet:

"A morsel, if I obtain it, is no gain, and a hunger, if I suffer it, is no gharam."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 25, verse 67:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are ever between that (middle course)﴾.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited this word as: ﴿وَلَمْ يُقْتِرُوا﴾ with a damma on the yā' (the first letter of the imperfect) and a kasra on the tā', the imperfect of aqtara (the quadriliteral form). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited it as: ﴿وَلَمْ يَقْتِرُوا﴾ with a fatha on the yā' and a kasra on the tā' fawqiyya, the imperfect of qatara (the triliteral form), like daraba. 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited it as: ﴿وَلَمْ يَقْتُرُوا﴾ with a fatha on the yā' and a damma on the tā' fawqiyya, the imperfect of qatara (the triliteral form), like nasara. The noun al-iqtar (in the recitation of Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir) and al-qatr (in the recitation of the rest) have the same meaning, which is restriction that harms and leaves a need unmet, the obligatory kind. Al-israf in His saying, "they were not extravagant," means exceeding the limit in spending.

Know that the most apparent of the views on this noble verse is that God praised His righteous servants for their moderation in spending: they do not exceed the limit through extravagance in spending, nor are they stingy (yaqturun), meaning they do not constrict and so withhold the required amount.

Some scholars said: extravagance in the verse is spending on what is unlawful and vain, and stinginess is withholding what is obligatory as a right. Although this meaning is true, the most apparent meaning in the verse is the first view.

Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, said: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy﴾, the verse, meaning: they are not wasteful in their spending, so as to spend beyond the need, nor miserly toward their families, so as to fall short in their rights and not provide for them; rather, (they are) just and choice, and the best of matters is the middle, neither this nor that. The relevant part of his words ends here.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and ever between that﴾, meaning: between that mentioned extravagance and constriction, (is) qawaman, meaning a just and middle course, free from the fault of extravagance and constriction.

The most apparent grammatical analysis in the verse, in my view, is what al-Qurtubi mentioned. He said: qawaman is the predicate (khabar) of (p-76) kana, and its subject is implied within it, meaning: spending was qawaman between extravagance and constriction. Then he said: this is what al-Farra' said. The remaining grammatical analyses of the verse are not sound in my view, such as the saying of one who said that the word bayn is the subject of kana and was not put in the nominative because it is built (mabni) due to its being attached to a built word; and the saying of one who said that bayn is the predicate of kana and qawaman is an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal) for it; and of one who said that both are predicates. All of that is not sound in my view, and the first is the more apparent.

The apparent meaning is that the moderation in spending for which He praised them includes their spending on their families and their spending of wealth in avenues of good.

This meaning indicated by this noble verse is clarified in other places. Among them: Allah enjoined His Prophet ﷺ to act in accordance with its requirement in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it completely outstretched﴾ [al-Isra': 29]. His saying, "do not make your hand chained to your neck," meaning withholding from spending in a total withholding, conveys the meaning of His saying here, "nor are they stingy." His saying, "nor extend it completely outstretched," conveys the meaning of His saying here, "they were not extravagant." God also pointed to this meaning in His saying: ﴿And give the relative his right, and the needy and the wayfarer, and do not squander wastefully﴾ [al-Isra': 26], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus﴾, the verse [al-Baqarah: 219], according to the more correct of the two explanations.

We have explained the verses indicating this meaning at the beginning of surah "al-Baqarah," in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3].

* *

Issue.

This noble verse, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy﴾, the verse, and the verses we mentioned with it, have clarified one of the two pillars of what is now called economics.

The clarification of that is that there is no disagreement among rational people that all issues of economics, despite their multiplicity and the variety of their types, return by the primary division to two origins, with no third to them.

The first of them: acquiring wealth.

The second of them: disbursing it in its proper channels. By this you know that economics is a dual action, and there is no benefit in either of the two origins mentioned except with the existence of the other. If a person were the best of people in considering the ways of acquiring wealth, but was the most foolish and ignorant of the ways of spending it, all the wealth he acquired would be lost to him without benefit. Likewise, if a person were the best of people in considering the spending of wealth in its productive channels, but was the most foolish and ignorant of the ways of acquiring it, his good consideration in spending would not benefit him, since he was unable to obtain anything to spend. The verses mentioned guided people and alerted them to economy in spending.

Once you know that all issues of economics return to the two origins mentioned, and that the verses mentioned indicated one of them, know that the other of them, which is acquiring wealth, is guided to by other verses that indicated God opening the doors to acquiring wealth by suitable means, such as trade and other things;

• like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198];

• and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse within the land and seek from the bounty of Allah﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10];

• and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He knows that there will be among you those who are ill, and others traveling throughout the land seeking from the bounty of Allah﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. The intended meaning of "the bounty of Allah" in the mentioned verses is the profit of trade;

• and like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except that it be trade by mutual consent among you﴾ [al-Nisa': 29]. We previously mentioned, in surah "al-Kahf," in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city﴾, the verse [al-Kahf: 19], the types of partnerships (shirkat) and their names, and we explained what is permissible among them and what is not permissible according to the four Imams, and we clarified what they agreed upon prohibiting, what they agreed upon permitting, and what they differed about. By this you know the multitude of ways that Allah opened for acquiring wealth by suitable lawful means.

Once you know from what we mentioned that all issues of economics return to two origins, namely acquiring wealth and disbursing it in its proper channels, know that each of these two origins necessarily requires two essential matters: The first of them: knowing the ruling of Allah concerning it, because Allah, mighty and exalted, did not permit acquiring wealth by all the means by which wealth is acquired, but permitted some means and forbade others, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has permitted trade and forbidden usury﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275]. Allah, mighty and exalted, did not permit spending wealth on everything, but permitted some spending and forbade some of it, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven spikes, in each spike a hundred grains﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261]. And He said regarding unlawful spending: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to avert from the way of Allah; they will spend it, and then it will be for them a regret﴾ (p-78) the verse [al-Anfal: 36]. Therefore, knowing the ruling of Allah regarding acquiring wealth and regarding spending it in its proper channels is an essential matter that is indispensable, because whoever does not know that may acquire wealth by an unlawful way, and wealth acquired by an unlawful way has absolutely no good in it; and he may spend wealth in an unlawful way, and spending it in that manner is a regret for its owner.

The second matter: knowing the means that suffice for acquiring wealth. A person may know, for example, that trade in a certain type is lawful according to the Shari'ah, but he does not know the ways of disposing of it in the interest that suffices for obtaining wealth from that lawful way. How many a dealer seeks profit, but his dealing returns to him with loss, because he does not know the ways by which profit is obtained. Likewise, a person may know that spending on a certain thing is permissible and has benefit in it, but he is not guided to knowing the proper manner of that spending, as is observed in many projects of great benefit if wealth is spent in them with wisdom and interest; the permissibility of spending in them is known, but carrying out the spending in the way of interest is not known to all people.

From this you know that the great foundations of economics are four. The first: knowing the ruling of Allah concerning the way by which wealth is acquired, and avoiding acquiring by it if it is prohibited by the Shari'ah.

The second: good consideration in acquiring wealth after knowing what the Creator of the heavens and the earth permits and what He does not permit.

The third: knowing the ruling of Allah concerning the ways in which wealth is spent, and avoiding the prohibited among them.

The fourth: good consideration in the ways of spending, and avoiding what is not beneficial among them. Whoever builds his economics upon these four foundations, his economics will suffice for his welfare and be pleasing to Allah, mighty and exalted. Whoever neglects one of these four foundations will be contrary to that, because whoever gathers wealth by means that Allah, mighty and exalted, does not permit, there is no good in his wealth and no blessing, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿Allah destroys usury and makes charities grow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 276], and He said, exalted is He: ﴿Say: not equal are the evil and the good, even if the abundance of the evil impresses you﴾, the verse [al-Ma'idah: 100].

We have discussed the issues of usury in the verse on usury in surah "al-Baqarah," and we discussed the types of partnerships and their names and explained what is permissible among them and what is not in surah "al-Kahf," in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city﴾, the verse [al-Kahf: 19].

(p-79) There is no doubt that it is incumbent upon Muslims in the regions of the world to cooperate upon an economics that the Creator of the heavens and the earth permits, through the tongue of His Messenger (ﷺ), and that is sufficient for knowing the ways of acquiring wealth by lawful means, and for disbursing it in its productive channels that are permitted by the Shari'ah. This is because the economics existing now in the regions of the world is not permitted by the noble Shari'ah, since those who organized its methods are not Muslims. The transactions of banks and companies contain nothing of it that is permissible by the Shari'ah, because they either include usurious increments, or contain gharar (uncertainty) with which a transaction is not permitted, such as the kinds of insurance commonly used by companies today in the regions of the world. You can hardly find any of them free from gharar, and the prohibition of gharar sale is established from the Prophet (ﷺ). It is well known that whoever claims the permissibility of the kinds of insurance known among companies, from the contemporary scholars, is mistaken in that, and because he has no evidence; rather, the sound proofs are contrary to what he says. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 25, verse 72:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity.﴾

That is: when they pass by the people of idle talk, and those who occupy themselves with it, they pass by turning away from them, with dignity, honouring themselves by refraining from plunging into their idle talk with them. Idle talk (lagh) is every speech in which there is no good, as has preceded.

This meaning which this noble verse indicates, the Exalted has clarified by His saying: ﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it and say: "To us our deeds, and to you your deeds. Peace be upon you. We do not seek the ignorant."﴾ [al-Qasas: 55]. We have already presented the verses that indicate the treatment of the servants of the Most Merciful towards the ignorant, in the surah of Maryam, in the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord"﴾ and the rest of the verse [Maryam: 47].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 25, verse 73:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the verses of their Lord, do not fall down before them deaf and blind﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Their not falling down before them is not a negation of the falling down; rather it is an affirmation of it, and a negation of deafness and blindness. It is like when you say: 'Zayd does not meet me greeting [me],' where the negation falls on the greeting, not on the meeting."

The meaning is: when they are reminded of them, they throw themselves upon them, eager to listen to them, and they turn towards the one who reminds them with them, and while they are throwing themselves upon them, they are hearing with attentive ears and seeing with watchful eyes. The point of relevance from it ends here.

It is not hidden that this noble verse has two indications: an indication by its explicit wording (manṭūq) and an indication by its implicit meaning (mafhūm). By its explicit wording it indicates that among the attributes of the servants of the Most Merciful is that when they are reminded of the verses of their Lord, they do not fall down before them, that is, they do not throw themselves upon them while being deaf to hearing what is in them of the truth, and blind to seeing it. Rather, they throw themselves upon them while hearing the truth in them and seeing it.

This meaning is indicated by other verses of the Book of Allah, such as His saying the Exalted: ﴿And when His verses are recited to them, it increases them in faith﴾ [al-Anfal: 2], and it is known that whoever has the verses of this Qur'an recited to him, and they increase him in faith, is not one who falls down upon them deaf and blind. And such as His saying the Exalted: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, among them are those who say, "Which of you has this increased in faith?" As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124], and His saying the Exalted: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book consistent, repeating; the skins shiver from it of those who fear their Lord; then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Zumar: 23], and others besides these verses.

The aforementioned verse also indicates by its implicit meaning that the disbelieving opponents of the servants of the Most Merciful described in these verses, when they are reminded of the verses of their Lord, fall down upon them deaf and blind, that is, they do not hear what is in them of the truth, nor see it, as though they had never heard them at all.

This meaning which this noble verse indicates by its implicit meaning has come clarified in other verses of the Book of Allah:

• Such as His saying the Exalted in Surah "Luqman": ﴿And when Our verses are recited to him, he turns away arrogantly, as if he had not heard them, as though in his ears is deafness. So give him tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Luqman: 7].

• And His saying the Exalted in "al-Jathiyah": ﴿Woe to every sinful liar﴾ ﴿who hears the verses of Allah recited to him, then persists arrogantly as though he had not heard them. So give him tidings of a painful punishment﴾ ﴿And when he learns of something of Our verses, he takes them in mockery; those will have a humiliating punishment﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 7–9].

• And His saying: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, among them are those who say, "Which of you has this increased in faith?" As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice﴾ ﴿And as for those in whose hearts is disease, it has increased them in defilement to their defilement﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124–125], and others besides these verses.

The apparent meaning is that the meaning of the disbelievers falling upon the verses, while they are deaf and blind, is their throwing themselves upon denying them and rejecting them, contrary to what al-Zamakhshari mentioned in "al-Kashshaf". The "ṣumm" in the verse is the plural of aṣamm (deaf), and "al-ʿumyān" is the plural of aʿmā (blind). And knowledge is with Allah the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 25, verse 75:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those will be rewarded with the high chamber (al-ghurfah) for what they endured with patience﴾. The apparent meaning of al-ghurfah in this noble verse is its genus, which encompasses many chambers (ghuraf), as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they will be secure in the chambers (al-ghurufat)﴾ [Saba': 37], and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For them are chambers, above them are chambers built high, beneath which rivers flow﴾ [az-Zumar: 20].

We have clarified this in the beginning of surah "al-Hajj" and elsewhere.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they will be met therein with greeting and peace﴾.

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in surah "Yunus," in the discussion of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Their greeting therein will be "Peace"﴾ [Yunus: 10].

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those will be rewarded with the high chamber (al-ghurfah) for what they endured with patience﴾, and the rest of the verse.

This noble verse indicates that they will be rewarded with one chamber, yet other verses have come that indicate otherwise, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For them are chambers, above them are chambers built high﴾ [az-Zumar: 20], and His saying: ﴿And they will be secure in the chambers (al-ghurufat)﴾ [Saba': 37].

The answer is that al-ghurfah here means al-ghuraf (the chambers), as already explained fully with its evidences in the discussion of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven and made them seven heavens﴾, and the rest of the verse [al-Baqarah: 29].

It has been said that al-ghurfah refers to the highest rank (ad-darajah al-'ulya) in Paradise, and on this view there is no difficulty. It has also been said: al-ghurfah is Paradise itself, named so because of its loftiness.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 25, verse 76:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Abiding therein; how good is it as a place of settlement and abode﴾.

We have already presented the verses that clarify this in Surah "al-Kahf," in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How excellent is the reward, and how good is it as a resting place﴾ [al-Kahf: 31].

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 25, verse 77:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication. But you have denied, so the punishment will be inevitable."﴾

The Arabs, in whose language the Qur'an was revealed, say: *ma 'abaftu bi-fulanin* (I did not care for so-and-so), meaning: *ma balaytu bihi* (I paid him no heed) and *wa-la iktaraθtu bihi* (I did not regard him), that is, he had no weight or value with me that would warrant my caring for him or paying him attention. Its root is from *al-'ib'* (burden), which is weight. From this is the saying of Abu Zayd describing a lion:

*Kāna bi-naḥrihi wa-bi-mankibayhi 'abīran, bāta ya'baʾuhu 'arūsu*

(On his chest and his shoulders was musk, which the bride would pile up on him through the night.)

His saying *ya'baʾuhu* means he places some of it upon some other, out of his care for it and his regard for it.

Knowing this, you should know that the statements of the exegetes on this noble verse revolve around four opinions.

Know first that the scholars differed concerning the verbal noun in His saying ﴿supplication (du'a'ukum)﴾: is it construed as an annexation to its agent (subject) or to its object? If it is annexed to its agent, then those addressed in the verse are the ones who supplicate, not the ones supplicated, meaning: ﴿My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication﴾, that is, your worship of Him. If the verbal noun is annexed to its object, then those addressed in the verse are the ones supplicated, not the ones who supplicate, meaning: He would not care for you were it not for His calling you to His Oneness and His worship through the tongues of His messengers, upon them be peace.

Know also that three of the four opinions mentioned concerning the verse are based on the verbal noun being annexed to its agent, and the fourth is based on it being annexed to its object.

As for the three opinions based on its being annexed to its agent:

The first of them is that the meaning is: ﴿My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication﴾, that is, your worship of Him alone, may He be exalted. According to this view, the address is general to the disbelievers and the believers, and then He singled out the disbelievers, excluding the believers, with His saying: ﴿But you have denied﴾, and so on.

The second of them: the meaning is: ﴿were it not for your supplication﴾, O disbelievers, directed to Him alone in times of hardship and distress, that is, even if you return to your polytheism once He has removed the harm from you.

The third: the meaning of ﴿My Lord would not care for you﴾ is that He would not do anything with your punishment were it not for your calling upon other gods along with Him. The weakness of this view is not hidden, and in it there is the assumption of something for which there is no evidence and no need.

As for the fourth opinion, based on the verbal noun in the verse being annexed to its object, it is evident: My Lord would not care for you were it not for His calling you through the tongues of His messengers.

Having understood these opinions, know that each one of them is supported by a Qur'anic text. Here, God willing, we will show the evidence from the Qur'an for each opinion, together with mention of what appears to us to be the most preponderant among them.

As for this last opinion, based on the verbal noun in the verse being annexed to its object, and that the meaning is: My Lord would not care for you were it not for His calling you to faith in Him, His Oneness, and His worship through the tongues of His messengers, it is supported by verses from the Book of God:

• such as His saying, may He be exalted, at the beginning of Surat Hud: ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water, that He might test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [al-Fatiha: 7]

• and His saying at the beginning of Surat al-Kahf: ﴿Indeed, We have made that which is upon the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed﴾ [al-Kahf: 7]

• and His saying at the beginning of Surat al-Mulk: (p-83) ﴿He who created death and life that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [al-Mulk: 2].

These verses have made clear that the wisdom in His creating the heavens and the earth, and all that is upon the earth, and death and life, is that He should call them through the tongues of His messengers and test them, that is, examine them as to which of them is best in deed.

These verses explain the meaning of His saying: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56].

In these verses there is clarification that the meaning of His saying ﴿were it not for your supplication﴾ is: His calling you through the tongues of His messengers, and your being tested as to which of you is best in deed. On this basis there is no difficulty in His saying ﴿But you have denied﴾, that is: (He would not care for you were it not for) His calling you, that is, and He has called you, but you denied. This view is the only one that is free of difficulty, and it is strong by the evidence of the verses mentioned.

As for the view that the meaning of ﴿were it not for your supplication﴾ is your sincerely calling upon Him, O disbelievers, in times of hardship and distress, its meaning is supported by many verses, such as His saying: ﴿So when they board the ship, they call upon God, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 65], and His saying: ﴿A violent wind came upon them, and the waves came at them from everywhere, and they thought they were encompassed, they called upon God, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [Ta-Ha: 22].

We have clarified the verses indicating this meaning in Surat Bani Isra'il, in the discussion of His saying: ﴿And when harm touches you at sea, those you call upon vanish except Him﴾ [al-Isra': 67]. Although many verses indicate this view, it does not appear that it is the meaning of this verse of al-Furqan.

As for the view that the meaning is: He would not do anything with your punishment were it not for your calling upon other gods along with Him, its meaning is indicated by His saying: ﴿What would God do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe?﴾ [al-Nisa': 147].

The first opinion, which is the most famous and has the most adherents, namely that the meaning is ﴿your supplication﴾, that is, your worship of Him alone, is indicated by all the verses that show what God gives to those who obey Him and what He has prepared for those who disobey Him, and their number is well known and not hidden.

Know that the particle *(ma)* in His saying ﴿Say: "My Lord would not care for you"﴾: some of the people of knowledge said it is interrogative, and some of them said it is negative, and both have a basis from the standpoint of analysis.

Know also that the statement of the one who said: ﴿were it not for your supplication﴾, that is, your supplicating Me that I might forgive you and give you what you ask, returns to the first opinion, because the supplication of request falls within worship, as is known. And His saying ﴿But you have denied﴾, that is, with what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) brought you.

We have already stated, in the discussion of His saying: ﴿Indeed, its punishment was ever adhering﴾ [al-Furqan: 65], that the meaning of His saying ﴿so the punishment will be inevitable﴾ is that the punishment will be constant for them, clinging to them, not separating from them, as its explanation has already preceded.

A group of the people of knowledge said: the intended meaning of the punishment that is inevitable for them, expressed by His saying "the punishment will be inevitable," is that what befell them of punishment on the Day of Badr, for seventy of them were killed and seventy were captured. Those of them who were killed suffered the punishment of killing, and the punishment of the barzakh (intermediate state) and the Hereafter joined with it, so it is constant and never separates from them in any state. That the *lizam* (inevitability) mentioned in this verse is the punishment that fell on the Day of Badr was related by Ibn Kathir from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, al-Suddi, and others. Then he said: al-Hasan al-Basri said: ﴿so the punishment will be inevitable﴾ means: on the Day of Resurrection, and there is no contradiction between them. End of quotation from Ibn Kathir. The author of *al-Durr al-Manthur* related it from most of those mentioned and others.

A group of the people of knowledge said: the Day of Badr is mentioned by God, may He be exalted, in verses of His Book. They said that it is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And We will surely make them taste from the lesser punishment﴾ [al-Sajdah: 21], that is, on the Day of Badr, ﴿short of the greater punishment﴾ [al-Sajdah: 21], that is, the Day of Resurrection. They said it is also what is meant by ﴿so the punishment will be inevitable﴾, and that it is what is meant by the seizing and retribution in His saying: ﴿On the Day We seize with the greatest seizure; indeed, We will take retribution﴾ [al-Dukhan: 16]. They said it is also the *Furqan* (criterion) that separates truth from falsehood in His saying: ﴿If you have believed in God and what We sent down upon Our servant on the Day of the Criterion, the Day the two armies met﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], which is the Day of Badr. And that it is the day in which victory came, in His saying: ﴿And God had already given you victory at Badr﴾ [Al 'Imran: 123]. That these mentioned verses refer to the Day of Badr is established in part in the *Sahih*, from Ibn Mas'ud. This is also what is meant by the statement of Shaykh Ahmad al-Badawi al-Shinqiti in his versified account of the military campaigns, in speaking of Badr, where he came with a passing allusion in mention:

*Li-annahu al-'adhābu wa-l-lizām*
(Because it is the punishment and the inevitability)

*Wa-annahu al-baṭshu wa-l-intiqām* ∗∗∗ *wa-annahu al-furqānu bayna al-kufri*
(And it is the seizing and the retribution; and it is the criterion between disbelief)

*Wa-l-ḥaqqi wa-l-naṣri sajīsa al-dahri* ∗∗∗
(And truth, and the victory, for the whole span of time.)

The meaning of *sajīsa al-dahr* is: its duration.

The most evident opinion concerning the verse, in my view, is that the verbal noun in it is annexed to its object, because it proceeds according to the eloquent language without difficulty or assumption. Among those who held this view was Qatadah, and God knows best.
